checks: The Minkowski average of two translated positive homothets of the same convex body has the averaged scale and translation. Equality of two such homothets identifies their scales by any positive directional width and identifies their translations by the centroid of the common shape at zero.

Rewriting a parent relation expresses each child base as an affine combination of its parent and an associated root. Termination shows the roots affinely span P. Reflections of all roots about the designated root form a centrally symmetric hull of full relative rank, so that root is in the relative interior of conv P. Rank zero is a singleton case.

The hull of the measured fibers is contained in the original convex body and contains its full prescribed fiber at every measured base. Thus the actual sampled fibers are unchanged. Positivity of Minkowski combinations also gives completeness of the positive integer base in its convex hull, as used only for the original note's downstream graph consequence.

The actual fiber support profile is concave in each fixed direction by convexity of the hull. At the relative interior root an affine majorant exists on the entire relative base domain. The midpoint identity in that direction makes the pair's nonnegative gaps sum to zero, forcing contact at every root, including the designated one.

Opposite direction majorants cancel the translation term, and division by the nonzero width of K gives one affine radius on roots. For the coordinate directions subtract the affine radius term from the matching majorants, giving each centroid coordinate. The exact parent identities propagate all these affine values to every site.

Source §4 graph and mixed depth are separate consequences of already accepted affine-selection statements, and §5 uses the additional abstract-tree data.

overlap.comparison: It assumes exact root-volume equality at every same-parity pair and derives their centroid midpoint identities and depth. It does not infer full affine radius and center data from one designated star and terminating forest.

It starts with a global affine root majorant, studies the tight sites and gives their centroid graph consequences. The frozen theorem constructs affine data over the entire positive sample using the directional star and forest, without assuming that majorant.

readability: The affine map at the roots is constructed using different directional majorants, then fixed before propagation. This avoids any general claim that the centroid commutes with arbitrary Minkowski addition.
